content:
- What did you change the port from, what to, and why?

- How long has this been going on?

It's difficult to tell from this error message exactly what the problem is. It implies two things:

- You have tried to authenticate too many time with a wrong password or OAuth2 token. This could happen if you have multiple devices checking or sending email, and one or more is sending the wrong password or is not OAuth2 authenticated. Have you changed your password recently? If you have been blocked for excessive wrong passwords, that might trigger the next part of the error message:

- Their SMTP (sending) server is truly not available, that they are having technical problems on their end. OR they have blocked you.

Difficulty with connection can also be due to local anti-virus/network security/VPN software. If you use any of those, try temporarily disabling them or creating an exception for Thunderbird.


Here are my working Comcast SMTP settings. How do they compare with yours?

IMAP (Incoming): Incoming Server Type: IMAP Mail Server Incoming Server Name: imap.comcast.net Port: 993 User Name: <my email address> Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: OAuth2

SMTP (Outgoing): SMTP Server Name: smtp.comcast.net Port: 465 Connection Security: SSL/TLS Authentication method: OAuth2 User Name: <my email address>

If you are set to authenticate by OAuth2, your authentication token may have expired. You can force a re-authentication by the following method:

- Make sure cookies are allowed (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Web Content | Accept cookies from sites>);

- Delete all cookies for that account (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Web Content | Show Cookies>);

- Delete all entries for that account from saved passwords (see <Settings | Privacy & Security | Passwords | Saved Passwords>);

Now restart Thunderbird. You will be asked for your credentials, an OAuth2 token will be set, and hopefully they will be accepted and mail transaction will resume.

content:
The only password that Thunderbird uses for itself is the optional one you can set to protect your saved passwords. If you have lost or forgotten that password, you cannot recover it - you'd have to delete all your passwords and re-authenticate all your accounts. This article described the feature in more detail:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/protect-your-thunderbird-passwords-primary-password

If you're talking about the password for the email account itself, and the account is authenticated by Normal Password, you may be able to discover it in Saved Passwords (see <Account Settings | Privacy & Security | Passwords | Saved Passwords>.) If the account is authenticated by OAuth2, and you have lost or forgotten the password, you will have to reset it on the email provider's web site.

content:
Is the old account IMAP or POP3?

If I understand what you're going for, I think I would approach it something like this...

- Set up the new email account in Thunderbird and make sure it's working the way you want it to;

- Set up your old service to forward all email to the new address. After that you will receive no more new mail at the old address, though the account will still be active;

- Move all your old folders to Local Folders, keeping the structure intact;

- Set your new POP account to download its new mail to the appropriate folder in the newly created Local folder.

- Eventually, after 12/15, your old account will be deactivated and you can remove it from Thunderbird;

- Optionally, you can move the folder hierarchy back inside the new POP3 account heading in the Folders List.

I don't understand your last point, but the Identities feature might do what you're looking for. See this article about how to set up and use them:

https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/kb/using-identities

My guess is your PC is actually attempting to use the same SMTP server for both accounts. This is a common problem but easily fixed. Try this:

  1. click to account settings pane
  2. highlight the account that does not send
  3. look in lower right where there is a button that says something such as 'edit SMTP server. CLick it and see if it is the correct email id. My guess is it is the email address of the other account, DO NOT change it because the other account uses it. Instead, on the same pane with the 'edit SMTP server' button, to the left of the button is a dropdown menu Click that and you should see all SMTP servers listed. find yours and set it for the account. If you have problems, post back.

content:
In case you're unclear about "accounts" in Thunderbird, you can have any number of accounts set up, and they will all appear listed in the Folders List and in Accounts Settings. Typically each account will be for a different email address. In this case you will temporarily, during the transition, have two accounts for the same address, the difference being that one is the existing POP3, the other the new IMAP.

- Yes, you can keep the same email address. The new "account" is just another connection to the same server mailbox, using a different protocol.

- Yes, your address book will be untouched.

- To restore a profile that's been previously backed up using the "Creating a backup of large profiles" method described in the article I cited above, you would open your profile folder (found in the same way you found it when backing up) and replace every file in that folder with the contents of your backup folder (COPY those files, don't MOVE them, so your backup copy will remain intact.) You need to be comfortable with working with files and folders.

- If you're talking specifically about the folders found in the "Local Folders" section of Thunderbird, the answer is "Yes," They will be preserved.

If you're talking about any folders found in the POP3 account's section, you should move those into "Local Folders" before deleting the POP account. Then, at your convenience, you can optionally move them to the IMAP account in small batches, to avoid the sever choking on the upload.

The Moz backup is not Mozilla item and I can't recommend it. To copy a profile from one pc to another, these steps work:


BACKUP

  1. ensure thunderbird is not running on old PC
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. this should open windows file explorer in Appdata\roaming folder
  4. highlight the Thunderbird folder and copy to external media

RESTORE

  1. ensure thunderbird is installed, run once, and NOT running on new PC
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. delete the thunderbird folder
  4. you should be in Appdata\roaming folder , copy&paste the exported Thunderbird folder there.

When done, you could remove the Spectrum account, No change in thunderbird. When you are ready to leave spectrum, do this:

  1. install the addon, importexporttools NG
  2. click file>offline>download to be sure that all spectrum messages are on pc
  3. highlight each folder in spectrum account to save, one at a time, and rightclick, select the importexport option to export mbox
  4. next, highlight Local Folders, rightclick, and, one at a time, rightclick and select importexport option to import mbox
  5. after doing that, spot check to ensure all messages are in Local Folders. Once done, you can remove the spectrum account.
  6. now, all spectrum messages are in Local Folders, If you want them on the Outlook account, highlight each folder, select all, and then right click and select COPY to desired outlook folder. Check that all content is on the outlook account, as uploading to IMAP can be problematic
  7. once all the message folders have been copied to outlook and you've verified them, you can delete the local folder

content:
Why would you do that? If everything is working, why redo it? Yes, it is a simple procedure.


BACKUP

  1. ensure thunderbird is not running
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. this should open windows file explorer in Appdata\roaming folder
  4. highlight the Thunderbird folder and copy to external media

RESTORE

  1. ensure thunderbird is installed, run once, and NOT running
  2. enter %appdata% in search window on task bar and press Enter key
  3. delete the thunderbird folder
  4. you should be in Appdata\roaming folder , copy&paste the exported Thunderbird folder there.
  5. start thunderbird and all should be there

content:
Local Folders, that is, folders located in the Local Folders hierarchy, are independent of all "real" email accounts. They persist no matter what accounts you add or delete. So, in your case, add the new account, then move or copy any folders and messages you want to keep from the old account to Local Folders. Finally delete the old, unused account.

You might want to make a backup copy of your Profile folder in the unlikely event that something unexpected happens. Actually, you should make regular backups of your Profile if your email collection is precious to you.

content:
I know very little about the Proton Bridge, but I see from their setup web page (<https://proton.me/support/protonmail-bridge-clients-windows-thunderbird>) that it inserts itself in the the operating system as a proxy server, after which you set Thunderbird up to direct its mail traffic through the Bridge rather than an external mail server. It also looks to me like Proton is, or acts like an IMAP server, which means there are copies of all messages on the server, so removing the account from Thunderbird poses no risk of data loss.

A few things I'd try... Here are some suggestions from a thread here a couple of years ago ( <https://support.mozilla.org/en-US/questions/1526364> ) at least one of which seems to have solved another user's similar complaint:

- Restart everything: It sounds basic, but try fully quitting Proton Bridge and Thunderbird, then restart your computer. Sometimes the bridge just gets stuck in a weird state.

- Check your login/session: Open Proton Bridge and make sure you're still logged into your Proton account. Sometimes after updates or reboots, the session expires and you have to log back in.

- Run Proton Bridge as Administrator: Right-click the Proton Bridge shortcut and choose “Run as administrator.” On Windows 11, this sometimes helps with network permissions.

- Check for app updates: Make sure you’re on the latest version of both Proton Bridge and Thunderbird. Proton especially pushes out bug fixes fairly regularly.

If this doesn't do the trick, try uninstalling Proton Bridge, rebooting the computer, then re-installing Proton Bridge.

Let us know how that all works out and we may have some other suggestions if necessary.
